findings.title: Missing authentication check on getDownloadFileSignedURL operation
findings.description: The getDownloadFileSignedURL operation in file-upload/operations.ts does not validate that the requesting user owns the file before generating a download URL. This allows any authenticated user to generate download URLs for any file in the system by guessing or knowing S3 keys.
findings.suggested_fix: Add authentication and authorization check: (1) Verify context.user exists with `if (!context.user) throw new HttpError(401)`. (2) Query the File entity to verify the file belongs to the authenticated user before generating the URL: `const file = await context.entities.File.findUnique({ where: { s3Key }, select: { userId: true } }); if (!file || file.userId !== context.user.id) throw new HttpError(403, 'File not found or access denied');`

findings.title: Missing RBAC check for admin dashboard access
findings.description: Admin dashboard pages (UsersDashboardPage, AnalyticsDashboardPage, SettingsPage) accept a user parameter but do not validate that the user has admin privileges. Any authenticated user who can navigate to /admin URLs could potentially access sensitive admin data.
findings.suggested_fix: Add admin role validation at the beginning of each admin page component: `if (!user.isAdmin) return <Navigate to="/" />`. Additionally, ensure the Wasp main.wasp file has `authRequired: true` set on all admin page routes. For server-side queries like getDailyStats, verify `if (!context.user?.isAdmin) throw new HttpError(403, 'Admin access required')` in the operation handler.

findings.title: Unauthenticated access to getDailyStats analytics query
findings.description: The getDailyStats operation is called from AnalyticsDashboardPage without visible authentication enforcement in the client code. If the server-side operation lacks proper authentication checks, sensitive analytics data could be exposed.

locations.snippet: const { data: stats, isLoading, error } = useQuery(getDailyStats);

findings.suggested_fix: Ensure getDailyStats operation (defined in server operations, not shown in provided code) has: (1) Authentication check: `if (!context.user) throw new HttpError(401)`. (2) Admin authorization check: `if (!context.user.isAdmin) throw new HttpError(403, 'Admin access required')`. (3) Mark the route as `authRequired: true` in main.wasp configuration.

findings.title: Cross-user file access via direct S3 key manipulation
findings.description: The FileUploadPage allows users to download files by setting s3Key state, which is then used in getDownloadFileSignedURL. Since getDownloadFileSignedURL doesn't validate file ownership, a user could modify the S3 key in browser DevTools to download other users' files.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass the file ID (not S3 key) to the download function instead: (1) Change download logic to pass file `id` instead of `s3Key`: `refetchDownloadUrl({ fileId: file.id })`. (2) Update getDownloadFileSignedURL to accept fileId, query the File entity, verify ownership, then generate the signed URL. This prevents users from bypassing ownership checks via direct S3 key manipulation.

findings.title: Weak password reset token validation flow
findings.description: The PasswordResetPage and RequestPasswordResetPage components use Wasp's built-in auth forms (ResetPasswordForm, ForgotPasswordForm) without visible token validation logic in the provided code. If the backend doesn't properly validate reset token expiration and one-time use, attackers could reuse or forge tokens.
findings.suggested_fix: Verify in Wasp's server-side auth configuration that: (1) Password reset tokens have a short expiration time (typically 15-30 minutes). (2) Tokens are single-use and deleted/invalidated immediately after being used. (3) Token generation uses cryptographically secure random values. (4) Tokens are stored securely (hashed) in the database. These are typically Wasp framework features, but confirm in main.wasp that `email.passwordResetTokenExpirationInMinutes` is set appropriately and token reuse is prevented.

findings.title: Admin role assignment based on email without validation
findings.description: The userSignupFields.ts file sets isAdmin=true based on matching email addresses from an ADMIN_EMAILS environment variable. However, there's no verification that the email is actually verified before assigning admin privileges, and email verification could be bypassed.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement post-signup email verification before granting admin access: (1) Initially set isAdmin=false for all signups. (2) After email verification is confirmed via EmailVerificationPage, have an admin manually verify and promote the user. (3) Alternatively, use a separate admin provisioning flow that requires verification. (4) For email-based auth methods, ensure the isAdmin assignment only happens after `emailVerified: true` is confirmed in the Wasp auth context.

findings.title: Email verification token sent in plaintext via email
findings.description: The getVerificationEmailContent function in emails.ts sends the full verification link (which includes the token) in plaintext in the email body. If email is intercepted or logs are accessed, the token is exposed.
findings.suggested_fix: This is inherent to email verification flows and Wasp handles this securely by default. However, ensure: (1) Verification links use HTTPS-only URLs. (2) Verification tokens are generated with `crypto.randomBytes()` or similar. (3) Tokens have short expiration (5-24 hours). (4) Consider adding rate limiting on email verification endpoints to prevent brute force. (5) Log email sends but never log the actual token/link. Wasp framework typically implements these, but verify in main.wasp configuration.

findings.title: OAuth provider email verification bypass for GitHub
findings.description: In getGitHubUserFields, the isAdmin check verifies email is verified, but the primary login flow doesn't enforce verified email status. A user could potentially register via GitHub without a verified email and later gain access to email-gated features.
findings.suggested_fix: Ensure email verification status is checked for all OAuth providers, not just for admin assignment: (1) Add a check in signup flow: `if (!emailInfo.verified) throw new Error('Email must be verified with GitHub')`. (2) Require unverified email users to verify via the app's email verification flow before accessing paid/restricted features. (3) Store emailVerified status in the User entity and enforce it at operation level, not just component level.

findings.title: Missing authentication on payment webhook endpoints
findings.description: The webhook.ts file exports paymentsWebhook and paymentsMiddlewareConfigFn, which should rely on signature verification from payment providers. However, if signature validation is misconfigured or missing, attackers could forge webhook events to grant subscriptions or credits without payment.
findings.suggested_fix: Verify in the specific payment processor webhook implementations (Stripe, LemonSqueezy, Polar) that: (1) All webhook events are validated using the provider's signature verification (e.g., Stripe uses `stripe.webhooks.constructEvent()`). (2) Webhook secrets are stored in environment variables and never hardcoded. (3) Webhook endpoint is registered with the payment processor to prevent forgery. (4) Only trusted event types are processed. Stripe webhook example at stripe/webhook.ts should have `stripe.webhooks.constructEvent()` call; verify it's present and properly configured.

findings.title: User data leakage in error messages on failed auth
findings.description: Auth pages (LoginPage, SignupPage) use Wasp's built-in auth forms which may expose whether an email exists in the system through different error messages (e.g., 'User already exists' vs 'Invalid credentials').
findings.suggested_fix: Review Wasp's authentication error handling. If possible in main.wasp configuration: (1) Use generic error messages on login failure ('Invalid email or password') instead of distinguishing between 'user not found' and 'wrong password'. (2) Ensure signup returns generic success message whether email exists or not. (3) For password reset, return generic 'Check your email' regardless of whether the email exists. (4) Implement rate limiting to prevent email enumeration attacks on login/signup endpoints.

findings.title: Insufficient input validation on S3 key generation
findings.description: The getS3Key function in s3Utils.ts uses user-supplied fileName to construct the S3 key. While it extracts only the extension, a malicious filename could still cause issues (e.g., path traversal attempts, although S3 keys are flat).
findings.suggested_fix: Validate the file extension more strictly: (1) Only allow extensions from the ALLOWED_FILE_TYPES list, not just any extension. (2) Sanitize extension to prevent injection: `const ext = path.extname(fileName).slice(1).toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, '');`. (3) Add maximum length check to prevent DoS: `if (fileName.length > 255) throw new Error('Filename too long');`. (4) The current approach is already relatively safe since path traversal is mitigated by using randomUUID, but explicit validation is better practice.

findings.title: Missing rate limiting on payment operations
findings.description: The generateCheckoutSession operation can be called repeatedly without rate limiting, potentially allowing attackers to create numerous checkout sessions (DoS) or spam payment provider APIs.
findings.suggested_fix: Implement rate limiting on payment operations: (1) Add a rate limiter middleware in Wasp configuration (if available) to limit generateCheckoutSession to N requests per user per time window (e.g., 5 requests per 5 minutes). (2) Alternatively, track recent checkout sessions in cache/database and reject if user has created too many in a time window. (3) Log checkout session creation attempts for fraud detection. (4) Consider adding CAPTCHA for repeated failed checkout attempts.

findings.title: Type safety: any-typed array in analytics
findings.description: In googleAnalyticsUtils.ts, an array is typed as `any[]` which bypasses TypeScript's type checking and can lead to runtime errors.

locations.snippet: let activeUsersPerReferrer: any[] = [];

findings.suggested_fix: Define a proper interface for the referrer data type: `interface ReferrerData { source: string; visitors: string; }` and use `ReferrerData[]` instead of `any[]`.

findings.title: Type safety: @ts-ignore usage in analytics
findings.description: Multiple `@ts-ignore` comments are used to suppress TypeScript errors, indicating underlying type issues that should be properly resolved.

locations.snippet: // @ts-ignore
// @ts-ignore
// @ts-ignore

findings.suggested_fix: Remove @ts-ignore comments and properly type the response objects. The `response.rows` and `metricValues` properties should have proper types from the Google Analytics Data client.

findings.title: Magic number: URL expiration timeout repeated across files
findings.description: The value 3600 (seconds) for signed URL expiration is hardcoded in multiple files. This should be a named constant.

locations.snippet: Expires: 3600,
return await getSignedUrl(s3Client, command, { expiresIn: 3600 });

findings.suggested_fix: Create a constants file (e.g., `src/shared/constants.ts`) with `export const SIGNED_URL_EXPIRATION_SECONDS = 3600;` and import it in both files.

findings.title: Magic number: Hardcoded redirect delay in CheckoutResultPage
findings.description: The redirect delay value 4000ms is hardcoded and used both as a constant and inline in the code, creating potential inconsistency.

locations.snippet: const ACCOUNT_PAGE_REDIRECT_DELAY_MS = 4000;
{ACCOUNT_PAGE_REDIRECT_DELAY_MS / 1000} seconds...

findings.suggested_fix: The constant is properly defined and used, but this pattern should be consistent across all timing-related values. Consider moving all timing constants to a shared location.

findings.title: Code duplication: Duplicate headers object in Plausible analytics
findings.description: A `headers` object with identical content is defined both at module level and within the `getPageviewsForDate` function, creating redundant code.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the local `headers` variable inside `getPageviewsForDate` and use the module-level `headers` constant directly, or pass it as a parameter if it needs to be reused differently.

findings.title: Inconsistent naming: Mixed camelCase and snake_case in analytics
findings.description: Some functions use camelCase (getDailyPageViews) while others use similar patterns inconsistently. The API keys are also named with inconsistent patterns (PLAUSIBLE_API_KEY vs GOOGLE_ANALYTICS_PROPERTY_ID).
findings.suggested_fix: Document the environment variable naming convention and ensure consistency. Consider creating a unified env config file that normalizes all environment variable access.

findings.title: Potential runtime error: Non-null assertions on env vars without validation
findings.description: Environment variables are accessed with non-null assertions (!) in multiple files. If these are not set, the application will crash at runtime rather than failing gracefully.

locations.snippet: Bucket: process.env.AWS_S3_FILES_BUCKET!,

findings.suggested_fix: Use the existing `requireNodeEnvVar` function from `../../server/utils` to validate env vars at startup, or create a config initialization that validates all required env vars before the app starts.

findings.title: Magic number: Hardcoded test card number in pricing page
findings.description: The Stripe test card number '4242 4242 4242 4242 4242' is hardcoded in the pricing page UI.

locations.snippet: 4242 4242 4242 4242 4242

findings.suggested_fix: Move this to a constants file or configuration. While this is a well-known test value, keeping it separate makes it easier to update and document.

findings.title: Inconsistent error handling: Different patterns across payment webhooks
findings.description: Each payment provider webhook (Stripe, LemonSqueezy, Polar) uses slightly different patterns for error logging and response. This inconsistency makes maintenance harder.
findings.suggested_fix: Create a shared utility function for webhook error logging that all payment providers can use, ensuring consistent error handling behavior.

findings.title: Magic string: Hardcoded 'today' date in Google Analytics
findings.description: The string 'today' is used as a date parameter in the Google Analytics query. While it works, using dynamic dates would be more robust.

locations.snippet: endDate: "today",

findings.suggested_fix: Consider adding a comment explaining that 'today' is a valid GA4 relative date, or create a constant for clarity.

findings.description: The `paymentPlanCards` object contains display data (name, price, features) that could be consolidated with the `paymentPlans` object in plans.ts
findings.suggested_fix: Consider consolidating plan metadata into a single source of truth, or at minimum ensure the `name` property in `paymentPlanCards` references the constant rather than duplicating `prettyPaymentPlanName()` calls.

findings.title: Type safety: Generic type parameter uses any in throttle function
findings.description: The throttleWithTrailingInvocation function accepts `...args: any[]` which bypasses type safety for the throttled function.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a generic type parameter to preserve the function's parameter types: `export function throttleWithTrailingInvocation<T extends (...args: any[]) => any>(fn: T, ...)` and return `T & { cancel: () => void }`.

findings.title: Inconsistent constant patterns in pricing page
findings.description: The pricing page mixes inline constant definition (bestDealPaymentPlanId) with paymentPlanCards object. The constant could be in plans.ts for consistency.

locations.snippet: const bestDealPaymentPlanId: PaymentPlanId = PaymentPlanId.Pro;

findings.suggested_fix: Consider moving `bestDealPaymentPlanId` to plans.ts as a constant export if it's a fixed value, or make it configurable via environment variables.

findings.title: God module: admin module exceeds 1800 LOC with mixed concerns
findings.description: The admin module contains 1800 LOC across 21 files with mixed responsibilities including layout components, dashboard pages, analytics, user management, and settings. This violates single responsibility principle and makes the module difficult to maintain and test. Components are tightly coupled through shared layout infrastructure.

locations.snippet: Admin module spans: layout/, dashboards/, elements/ with mixed concerns

findings.suggested_fix: Split admin into domain-specific modules: admin-layout (shared UI infrastructure), admin-analytics (analytics dashboard + cards), admin-users (user management), admin-settings (settings management). Move analytics logic to dedicated analytics module.

findings.title: God module: payment module exceeds 1200 LOC with multiple provider integrations
findings.description: The payment module contains 1200 LOC across 21 files with three separate payment provider implementations (Stripe, LemonSqueezy, Polar), each with duplicate webhook, checkout, and payment processor logic. While providers are separated into folders, there's substantial code duplication and the module orchestrates multiple payment flows.

locations.snippet: Payment module contains: stripe/, lemonSqueezy/, polar/ with duplicated patterns

findings.suggested_fix: Create a payment provider abstraction layer with unified interfaces: IPaymentProcessor, ICheckoutUtils, IWebhookHandler. Extract common webhook validation logic into shared utilities. Consider a factory pattern to instantiate providers based on configuration.

findings.title: Missing abstraction layer between admin/payment pages and analytics operations
findings.description: Admin dashboard pages (AnalyticsDashboardPage, TotalRevenueCard, TotalSignupsCard) directly import analytics/operations.ts. Analytics operations contain business logic for fetching and aggregating user data. Changes to analytics logic require updating multiple dashboard components, creating tight coupling.

locations.snippet: TotalRevenueCard.tsx, TotalSignupsCard.tsx, AnalyticsDashboardPage.tsx directly call analytics/operations
Analytics operations expose business logic directly to UI layer

findings.suggested_fix: Create an analytics service/facade layer that abstracts operation queries. Dashboard components should consume high-level analytics data contracts rather than calling operations directly. This allows analytics logic to evolve independently.

findings.title: Client module exhibits high internal cohesion with unclear responsibilities
findings.description: The client module contains 2500 LOC across 34 files including app shell (App.tsx), routing, theming (DarkModeSwitcher), UI component library (30+ Radix UI wrapper components), hooks (useColorMode, useIsLandingPage, use-toast, useLocalStorage, useDebounce), navbar, and cookie consent. This creates a monolithic module where unrelated concerns are bundled together.

locations.snippet: Client module mixes: App.tsx (routing), hooks/, components/ui/, components/NavBar/, components/cookie-consent/

findings.suggested_fix: Reorganize client module: (1) Extract UI component library to separate 'ui-components' module, (2) Move App.tsx and routing to dedicated 'app-shell' module, (3) Create 'hooks' as sibling module to client, (4) Move NavBar and cookie-consent to 'layout' module or separate feature modules.

findings.title: Tight coupling between payment providers and checkout/PricingPage
findings.description: The PricingPage.tsx directly imports from payment/paymentProcessor.ts and specific provider implementations. Changes to payment provider selection logic or provider instantiation require modifying the UI component. No clear separation between payment UI orchestration and provider selection.

locations.snippet: PricingPage imports paymentProcessor and possibly provider-specific utils
Payment processor instantiation logic tightly coupled to page

findings.suggested_fix: Create a payment configuration/factory service that handles provider selection based on environment variables. PricingPage should only import a generic PaymentCheckoutService interface, delegating provider instantiation to the factory.

findings.title: No clear service layer between UI components and database operations
findings.description: Multiple modules (user, file-upload, demo-ai-app) define operations.ts files that directly handle database queries and business logic. Components import these operations directly without an intermediate service abstraction. This creates tight coupling between UI and data access patterns.

locations.snippet: User operations directly exposed to UI components
File upload operations directly exposed to FileUploadPage
Demo app operations directly exposed to DemoAppPage (487 LOC)

findings.suggested_fix: Create a consistent service/domain layer for each feature: UserService, FileUploadService, DemoAppService. These services should encapsulate operations.ts logic and expose clean interfaces. Components should depend on services, not operations.

findings.title: DemoAppPage exhibits god component pattern with 487 LOC
findings.description: The DemoAppPage.tsx contains 487 lines of code handling UI rendering, state management, scheduling logic, and potentially API integration. This file is substantially larger than typical React components and likely contains multiple responsibilities that should be decomposed.

locations.snippet: Large monolithic component file

findings.suggested_fix: Decompose DemoAppPage into smaller focused components: DemoAppLayout, ScheduleForm, ResultsDisplay, etc. Extract state management into a custom hook (useDemoAppState). Move scheduling logic to schedule.ts. Each sub-component should have single responsibility.

findings.title: Inconsistent error handling and validation patterns across modules
findings.description: Different modules handle validation and errors differently: payment/errors.ts, file-upload/validation.ts, server/validation.ts exist without clear cohesion. No unified validation or error handling framework across the application. Auth module uses userSignupFields.ts for form fields while other modules handle validation ad-hoc.

locations.snippet: Payment error definitions
File upload validation
Server-side validation
Auth field definitions mixed with validation

findings.suggested_fix: Create a shared validation module with reusable validators and error types. Consolidate validation logic across auth, payment, file-upload modules. Define application-wide error handling contracts.

findings.title: Landing page and blog modules lack clear separation from main app
findings.description: Landing page (1100 LOC) and blog (800 LOC) exist as separate modules but share UI components, styling, and potentially utilities with main client application. No clear boundary between marketing content and SaaS application. Blog is Astro-based while app is React, creating framework heterogeneity.

locations.snippet: Landing page contains 17 files with component duplication risk
Astro-based blog separate from React app

findings.suggested_fix: Consider whether landing page should be served from main React app or remain static. If static, establish clear API contracts for data. For blog, document whether Astro is intentional for static generation. Create shared design token system if components are duplicated.

findings.title: Analytics module tightly coupled to admin dashboard without provider abstraction
findings.description: Analytics module contains provider-specific implementations (googleAnalyticsUtils.ts, plausibleAnalyticsUtils.ts) but admin dashboard components directly depend on these specifics. No provider-agnostic analytics service interface. Provider switching requires changes to multiple dashboard components.

locations.snippet: Google Analytics provider implementation
Plausible Analytics provider implementation
Analytics operations potentially importing from specific providers

findings.suggested_fix: Create a provider abstraction layer (IAnalyticsProvider interface) that both Google Analytics and Plausible implement. Analytics operations should depend on abstraction, not concrete implementations. Admin dashboard should only depend on operations.ts.
